title: No JWT Token Revocation Mechanism
description: Logout only writes an audit log entry; the JWT access token remains valid until expiry. Refresh tokens also remain valid. A stolen token cannot be revoked server-side. The default access token lifetime is 30 days (configurable, with .env.example suggesting 30d access / 60d refresh).
evidence: src/auth/auth.service.ts L238-255 — logout() method only creates an audit log. src/auth/strategies/jwt.strategy.ts — no revocation check in validate(). No token-blacklist table, bloom filter, or short-expiry pattern exists anywhere.
impact: A compromised JWT grants indefinite access to the victim's account (all properties, tenants, financial data) for up to 30–60 days unless the database secret is rotated, which would invalidate ALL users' tokens simultaneously.
fix: Implement a token blacklist (Redis or DB table) checked in JwtStrategy.validate(). Alternatively, issue short-lived access tokens (5-15 min) with refresh token rotation. Set refresh token expiry shorter (e.g. 7 days).

title: In-Memory OTP/Reset Session Store — No Persistence, No Horizontal Scaling
cwe: CWE-613 (session fixation / expiry not enforced per-instance)
description: OTP codes and reset authorization tokens are stored in in-memory Maps (pendingOtps, resetSessions) inside the Node.js process. This means: (1) A server restart wipes all pending password resets, (2) Multiple API instances behind a load balancer cannot share OTP/reset state, (3) Process restarts during a reset flow leave the user in a broken state.
evidence: src/auth/auth.service.ts L43-44: private readonly pendingOtps = new Map<string, PendingOtpRecord>(); private readonly resetSessions = new Map<string, ResetSessionRecord>(); These are not persisted to Redis or the database.
impact: In production with multiple instances, password-reset flows randomly fail depending on which instance handles the request. A server restart during an active reset invalidates all outstanding OTPs — users must restart the flow.
fix: Replace in-memory Maps with a Redis-backed store (e.g. using @nestjs/bull or ioredis) for OTP validity and reset sessions. Set TTLs to match the existing 10-minute expiry.

title: JWT Payload Contains PII (Email, Phone)
description: The JWT payload includes email and phone fields in addition to sub and role. These are not encrypted in the JWT body (only base64-encoded, not encrypted unless using JWE). Any party with access to the token — browser extensions, analytics scripts, proxies — can read the user's email and phone number.
evidence: src/auth/auth.service.ts L628: const payload = { sub: userId, role, email, phone }; The email and phone fields are included even if null; they are available to any JWT decoder.
impact: PII exposure through JWT tokens that are sent in every HTTP request header. Email/phone leak if a token is intercepted, logged, or stored in a compromised location.
fix: Remove email and phone from JWT payload. Store only sub (userId) and role. Fetch user details from the database in the strategy's validate() method (already done). This also reduces JWT size.

title: Supabase Service Role Key Exposed in Backend — No User-Level Row-Level Security
description: The Supabase client is initialized with the service_role_key, which bypasses all Row-Level Security (RLS) policies in Supabase. While the API verifies ownership before generating upload/download URLs, a compromised API server grants full access to ALL Supabase Storage buckets without RLS restrictions.
evidence: src/files/storage/supabase-storage.service.ts L29-31: this.client = createClient(url, key, { auth: { persistSession: false } }); The service_role_key from config gives admin-level access.
impact: If an attacker gains access to the API server environment or the service_role_key, they have unrestricted read/write/delete access to all file buckets. Also, there is no per-user audit trail at the storage layer — visibility relies entirely on the API middleware.
fix: For user-owned files, use user-scoped Supabase tokens instead of the service role key. Use Supabase's built-in RLS policies with auth.uid() checks. Alternatively, keep the service role key but ensure strict environment isolation and rotate the key regularly.

title: ResetPasswordDirect Endpoint — Unauthenticated Password Change with Only Identifier + Current Password
description: The /auth/reset-password-direct endpoint is marked @Public() (no JWT required) and allows password change by providing an identifier (email/phone) + current password. While this is designed as a convenience for users who know their current password, it exposes a password-change operation without requiring the user to be authenticated via JWT. The endpoint is rate-limited (5/min), but an attacker who has both identifier and current password can change the password.
evidence: src/auth/auth.controller.ts L154-167: @Public() @Post('reset-password-direct') ... async resetPasswordDirect(@Body() dto: ResetPasswordDirectDto, @Req() req: Request). The flow does not check for an active JWT session.
impact: If an attacker compromises both the identifier (email/phone) and current password (e.g. via phishing, credential stuffing), they can change the password without triggering any second-factor verification or session invalidation. The same endpoint is usable from any unauthenticated context, making it a risk if credentials are compromised.
fix: Option A: Require JWT authentication (remove @Public()) and merge with change-password. Option B: Keep as public but send an email notification and enforce strict rate limiting. Option C: Require the refresh token body as an additional proof of recent authentication.

title: Hardcoded Development Fallback for RESEND_API_KEY Using process.env
affected_assets.description: Email service reads RESEND_API_KEY and RESEND_FROM directly from process.env in addition to ConfigService, bypassing the environment validation schema defined in env.validation.ts. This means misconfigured servers could use fallback values or fail silently.
affected_assets.evidence: Email Service L20-22: this.configService.get('RESEND_API_KEY') || process.env.RESEND_API_KEY; Email Service L40-42: process.env.RESEND_FROM || 'BariVara <onboarding@resend.dev>' The env.validation.ts schema has RESEND_API_KEY as @IsOptional() @IsString() with no @IsNotEmpty() — so it's not validated.
affected_assets.impact: Low risk. If RESEND_API_KEY is not set via ConfigService but IS set in the environment, it still works. However, if neither is set, OTP emails silently log to console in dev mode, and the forgot-password flow appears to succeed but no email is delivered. In production, this means password resets silently fail.
affected_assets.fix: Add RESEND_API_KEY to env.validation.ts as @ValidateIf non-test @IsString @IsNotEmpty. Use ConfigService exclusively — remove process.env fallback. Fail loudly in production if email is not configured.

affected_assets.title: Next.js App Has No Custom Security Headers (CSP, HSTS, X-Frame-Options)
affected_assets.description: The Next.js app uses the default next.config.ts with no security-related headers. There is no Content-Security-Policy, Strict-Transport-Security, X-Frame-Options, X-Content-Type-Options, or Referrer-Policy configured. While the API uses helmet, the frontend does not provide equivalent protections.
affected_assets.evidence: barivara-web/next.config.ts: export default nextConfig; with no headers() configuration. The frontend serves HTML that is not protected by CSP, making it potentially vulnerable to XSS if any user input is rendered unsafely.
affected_assets.impact: Increased attack surface for cross-site scripting, clickjacking, and MIME-type confusion attacks. Users accessing the app via HTTP (in dev) receive no HSTS protection.
affected_assets.fix: Add Content-Security-Policy, X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff, X-Frame-Options: DENY, Strict-Transport-Security (in production), and Referrer-Policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin to next.config.ts using the headers() function in Next.js App Router.

affected_assets.title: JWT Token Lifetime Defaults Are Extremely Long (30–60 Days)
affected_assets.description: The .env.example sets JWT_ACCESS_EXPIRES_IN=30d and JWT_REFRESH_EXPIRES_IN=60d, which are unusually long compared to industry standards (15 min access, 7 day refresh). Combined with the lack of token revocation (F-001), this means a compromised token is valid for 30 days.
affected_assets.impact: Extended window of exposure for stolen tokens. Financial data (rents, payments, tenant PII) is accessible for the full token lifetime.
affected_assets.fix: Reduce access token lifetime to 5–15 minutes, refresh token to 7 days. Implement refresh token rotation (invalidate old refresh tokens on each use). Add a lastPasswordChanged check to invalidate tokens after password change.

affected_assets.title: Audit Log Metadata Contains Email in Plain Text
affected_assets.description: The forgot-password audit log entry includes the user's email in the metadata field. While the registration audit log deliberately avoids PII in metadata (line 112 comment: 'no PII in metadata'), the forgot-password audit entry does include email.
affected_assets.evidence: src/auth/auth.service.ts L405: metadata: { action: 'FORGOT_PASSWORD_REQUEST', email: user.email }. Contrast with register L120: metadata: { action: 'REGISTER' } with no PII.
affected_assets.impact: If audit logs are compromised, an attacker can associate emails with password-reset events, potentially targeting users who recently reset passwords.
affected_assets.fix: Remove email from audit log metadata for forgot-password events, or hash it. The action itself is sufficient for audit purposes.
